title: With Due Respect (Vol. 6) -- Ch. 4: My Choices for May 10
keywords: a grand deception... a gigantic fraud
Ethical Standards Law for public officers
primary_topics: Chapter 4 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 6) -- CJP's April 25, 2010 Inquirer column answering 'whom will you vote for?' not by naming choices but by spelling out the three leadership attributes he seeks, summed in the keyword 'TIP': trust, integrity, and probity

Trust -- that 'good governance begins with the trust of the people,' that leading a democracy means hearing the minority and respecting rights, and his emphatic answer (against authoritarian temptation) that Filipinos can and do follow the rule of law, so a 'credible election' is essential to trust

Integrity -- distinguishing the corrupt, the merely 'honest' who tolerate surrounding evil, and the leaders of true integrity who have 'the moral courage to punish the greedy, chase the robbers, and prosecute the tyrants'

Probity -- defined beyond intellect as doing 'the right thing in the right way at the right time and for the right reasons,' illustrated by the abuse of Charter change through the 'grand deception' people's initiative (Lambino v. Comelec) pursued 'via the wrong method, at the wrong time, and for the wrong reasons'
sub_topics: The framing: with May 10 near, CJP answers readers 'not by naming my choices but by describing the attributes I am looking for,' attributes he had set out at the Management Association of the Philippines induction

Trust, first and foremost: 'good governance begins with the trust of the people'; democracy is hard because 'before decisions are taken, the minority must be heard; due process observed; public opinion heeded; constitutional rights respected,' and 'when human rights are transgressed, one individual prevails over the entire government'

Faith in democracy: against those who 'look to authoritarian regimes for economic salvation,' CJP insists Filipinos 'will never exchange their freedom for food' and will follow the rule of law -- proof being overseas Filipinos who 'stop at red lights even in deserted street corners,' pay correct taxes, and prosper -- so trust 'begins with [a] credible election,' making May 10 critical to 'the very survival of our democracy'

Integrity -- the three kinds of officials: the first 'arrogate absolute power... and amass ill-gotten wealth'; the second keep 'personally pure' yet 'do nothing to stamp out the evil around them'; and the third, whom the country needs, have 'the moral courage to punish the greedy, chase the robbers, and prosecute the tyrants'

Integrity defined: more than honesty ('a virtue taught in grade school'), it is the integrity 'that does not compromise with evil,' that 'underlies all canons of professional ethics,' and that 'backstops the Ethical Standards Law' -- leaders who work 'at the risk of their own safety, health... and careers' to 'safeguard liberty' and 'vindicate the poor'

Probity defined: not 'mere intellectuality' but, per Webster, 'uncompromising adherence to the highest principles or ideals' -- to which CJP adds 'the ability to discern various alternatives and to select the best,' doing 'the right thing in the right way at the right time and for the right reasons' (process, timing and motive mattering 'as much as substance')

The Cha-cha illustration: amending an imperfect 1987 Constitution is 'the right thing,' but leaders 'totally devoid of probity' pursued it the wrong way -- the people's initiative built on 'invented signatures,' which the Court (Lambino v. Comelec, 2006) called a 'grand deception' and a 'gigantic fraud' -- and the constituent-assembly push for a joint vote, 'at the wrong time' and 'for the wrong reason, to extend... the most unpopular president in history'
The mnemonic: CJP coins 'TIP' -- trust, integrity, probity -- as the 'three values... indispensable to win the future'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 4 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 6), CJP's April 25, 2010 Inquirer column, answers 'whom will you vote for?' not by naming choices but by spelling out three leadership attributes, summed in the keyword 'TIP': trust, integrity, and probity. On trust -- 'good governance begins with the trust of the people' -- he stresses that leading a democracy means the 'minority must be heard; due process observed... constitutional rights respected,' and against those tempted by authoritarianism he insists Filipinos 'will never exchange their freedom for food' and do follow the rule of law (overseas Pinoys 'stop at red lights even in deserted street corners' and pay correct taxes), so a 'credible election' is the foundation of trust and May 10 is critical to 'the very survival of our democracy.' On integrity, he sorts officials into three kinds -- the plunderers; the merely 'honest' who keep clean yet 'do nothing to stamp out the evil around them'; and the leaders the country needs, who have 'the moral courage to punish the greedy, chase the robbers, and prosecute the tyrants' -- an integrity that 'does not compromise with evil' and 'backstops the Ethical Standards Law.' On probity, he goes beyond intellect to Webster's 'uncompromising adherence to the highest principles,' adding the ability to do 'the right thing in the right way at the right time and for the right reasons,' since process, timing and motive matter as much as substance. His illustration: amending the imperfect 1987 Constitution is 'the right thing,' but leaders 'devoid of probity' pursued it the wrong way -- the people's initiative built on 'invented signatures' that the Court (Lambino v. Comelec) branded a 'grand deception' and a 'gigantic fraud,' and a constituent-assembly push 'at the wrong time' and 'for the wrong reason, to extend... the most unpopular president in history.' Hence his mnemonic, TIP -- trust, integrity, probity -- the 'three values... indispensable to win the future.'
